A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VQ-VAE-based investigation of language-model planning, despite the changed title and framing. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v1 reports original CFG, path-finding, and OpenWebText experiments, including mutual-information measurements, path-finding accuracy, and appendix validation and reconstruction results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds harder validation experiments, larger-model measurements, and empirical probe comparisons.

M1.justification: The proposed VQ-VAE architecture, code construction, four-part training objective, and planning-analysis pipeline are retained. Quantization and entropy regularization become explicit in Section 2 but already appear in v1 Appendix A. The additional estimator checks supplement the statistical assessment of this pipeline.

E1.justification: The CFG, PF-Short, PF-Long, and OpenWebText coverage remains. Appendix A.4 adds controlled validation scenarios involving single-token perturbations with Gaussian noise and unrelated prefixes sharing a latent label. These extend input conditions within the existing synthetic validation setting.

E2.justification: v1 discusses probing without evaluating probe baselines. v2 Appendices D.2 and D.5 evaluate two-layer MLP token-prediction and hidden-state-regression probes, plus predictive ν-information. The latter is also tested against the original known-MI validation setting, substantially expanding actual comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 24-layer, width-1024, greater-than-0.3B-parameter CFG model; separately trained probes for future offsets with accuracy and normalized-MSE evaluation; and validation with 16 surrogates per label and codebooks up to 2048. These are added experimental settings, not demonstrated reruns of the retained main experiments.

E4.justification: The single known-MI validation in v1 is extended with perturbation/noise and unrelated-surrogate stress tests. v2 also checks the horizon finding at larger model scale, analyzes probe behavior across offsets and training iterations, and reports agreement between alternative MI estimators.

E5.justification: Appendix E newly addresses finite-sample bias, variance, and MSE, reports use of bias-corrected plug-in and Paninski BUB estimators, and states that their estimates agree. Existing multiple-seed and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting is retained; no increased run count is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original horizon, history, codebook, and reconstruction results are retained. New Figures 6–7 and 17–20 report harder-validation results, rapid horizon decay for the larger model, probe outcomes, and ν-information failing to track reference MI. These are additional findings, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Appendices D.3–D.4 add mathematical counterexamples concerning probe losses and target rescaling; Appendix E adds estimator assumptions, asymptotic expressions, corrections, and bounds. However, Equation 7 predicts negative plug-in MI bias even at independence, where empirical MI is nonnegative, and Equation 10 consequently applies the correction with the wrong sign.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the planning contribution from three properties to horizon and branch awareness, recasting computational history as a separate diagnostic application. The revised conclusion also explicitly states that there are no consistent NTP–MTP differences, qualifying v1's emphasis on training-objective effects.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits MI interpretation to comparative dependence rather than a direct planning score and reframes Section 3.3 as information localization. Appendices A.3 and D add substantive explanations about hyperparameter limits, probe confounding, and purported resistance to rescaling, extending the earlier interpretation and limitations.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 specifies encoder training and reuse, optimization budgets, sequence counts, and configuration-file access. The reproducibility statement reports supplementary code, dataset-acquisition tools, and experiment instructions. These materially expand documentation; they do not establish changed budgets for existing experiments or independently verify the supplementary resources.

R1.justification: v2 adds Wu et al. on planning ahead, Xu et al. on usable information, and three references concerning information estimation. It develops a focused contrast with predictive ν-information while retaining the broader positioning against probing and mechanistic interpretability.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution framing, method exposition, Section 3.3 question, and conclusion are substantially revised. Section 2 gains a stepwise pipeline explanation and previously appended mathematical details. Validation is reorganized into subsections, and citations switch from numerical to author–date format.

P2.justification: v2 adds a pipeline diagram and six experimental figures, rearranges and frames the experimental-overview panels, and relocates existing appendix plots alongside their discussion. The conference layout changes typography, text width, and figure sizing. Retained heatmaps and Table 1 preserve their underlying results.

improvement.justification: The harder validation tests, larger-model replication, probe comparisons, and training documentation strengthen the evidence and reproducibility relative to v1. However, the new Appendix E reverses the plug-in MI bias and correction signs, undermining its statistical justification. The PDFs do not establish whether this error affected the implemented estimates. These substantive gains and unresolved methodological harms prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
